o: We scan prefixes of `nums` from left to right and want the longest prefix where deleting **exactly one** element makes every distinct value occur the same number of times. For example 1, the prefix of length 7 is `[2,2,1,1,5,3,3]`: removing the single `5` leaves each of `2,1,3` appearing twice. In example 2, the whole array works because removing the lone `5` makes `1,2,3,4` each appear three times. With $n$ up to $10^5$, an $O(n^2)$ check per prefix is too slow in the worst case, so we need a way to test validity in $O(1)$ as the prefix grows — which suggests maintaining frequency statistics incrementally.
k: A prefix is fixable by removing one element only in three cases: all counts are 1; exactly one value has count 1 and all others share one common count; or exactly one value has the maximum count and all others have maxCount - 1.
Maintaining `count[value]` plus `freqCount[c]` = how many values currently have count `c` lets us re-check validity in O(1) after each element.
The answer is monotone to compute online: after appending each element, update counters and record the current length if the prefix is still valid.

a.i: For each prefix length L, count occurrences of each value in that prefix, then try removing each distinct value present and check whether all remaining counts are equal. This directly mirrors the problem statement and is easy to reason about, but recounting for every prefix costs $O(n^2)$ overall, which TLEs at $n = 10^5$. It is still useful as a correctness reference for testing the optimal solution.
s: For each prefix length L from n down to 2:
Build a counter of values within nums[0..L).
For each distinct value v in the counter, decrement its count (simulating removal); if all remaining counts are equal, return L.
a.t: O(n^2) expected time — for each of n prefix lengths we rebuild a hash map and scan it.
a.sp: O(n) — the counter for one prefix holds up to n distinct values.

a.i: Grow the prefix one element at a time while maintaining `cnt[v]` (occurrences of v so far), `freq[c]` (how many values have count c), `maxF` (the maximum count), and `d` (number of distinct values). After each insertion the prefix can be fixed by one removal iff one of three shapes holds: (a) `maxF == 1` — remove any element; (b) exactly one value has count 1 and all other d-1 values have count `maxF` — remove that singleton; (c) exactly one value has count `maxF` and the other d-1 values have count `maxF - 1` — remove one occurrence of the max-count value. Each check is O(1), giving linear total time.
s: Initialize cnt, freq maps, maxF = 0, d = 0, ans = 0.
For each x: decrement freq[cnt[x]] if nonzero, increment cnt[x], increment freq[cnt[x]]; if cnt[x] was 0 before, d++; update maxF = max(maxF, cnt[x]).
Check validity: maxF == 1, or freq[1] == 1 && freq[maxF] == d - 1, or freq[maxF] == 1 && freq[maxF - 1] == d - 1.
If valid, set ans = current prefix length.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def maxEqualFreq(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        cnt = defaultdict(int)
        freq = defaultdict(int)
        maxF = d = ans = 0
        for i, x in enumerate(nums):
            if cnt[x] > 0:
                freq[cnt[x]] -= 1
            else:
                d += 1
            cnt[x] += 1
            freq[cnt[x]] += 1
            maxF = max(maxF, cnt[x])
            if (maxF == 1 or
                (freq[1] == 1 and freq[maxF] == d - 1) or
                (freq[maxF] == 1 and freq[maxF - 1] == d - 1)):
                ans = i + 1
        return ans

a.t: O(n) — each element triggers O(1) map updates and validity checks.
a.sp: O(n) — the two hash maps hold at most n entries combined.

w: In an interview, mention the brute force briefly to show you understand the problem, then pivot to the incremental counting solution since it is the intended $O(n)$ answer. Common pitfalls: forgetting that removing an element may leave zero elements (still valid, handled naturally since a length-1 prefix always passes via `maxF == 1`); off-by-one errors in the condition `freq[maxF] == d - 1` when there is only one distinct value; and not updating `maxF` correctly (it never needs to decrease during a forward scan since counts only grow). Edge cases to test: `[1,1]`, `[1,2,3,4]`, `[10,2,8,9,3,8,7,7,6,4,10,4]`. A likely follow-up: what if you could remove k elements instead of one — then the case analysis generalizes but becomes much harder, typically requiring different bookkeeping.
